title: What to Do When Someone Dies in Myanmar: 5-Step Official Checklist
titleEn: What to Do When Someone Dies in Myanmar: 5-Step Official Checklist
cardSummary: Official 5-step bereavement checklist for Myanmar: medical death certification, civil death registration, funeral and repatriation permits, survivor benefits, and estate succession.
introHtml: Handling legal and administrative tasks after a death in Myanmar requires direct local coordination because ongoing armed conflict and restricted or unreliable domestic ministry web infrastructure mean many Myanmar government portals (including Ministry of Health and Social Security Board websites) are offline, returning incomplete pages, or geo-restricted from abroad [1][2]. Accordingly, primary statutory rules covering Births and Deaths Registration, the Burma Laws Act 1898, the Succession Act, and the Social Security Law 2012 are anchored here in ILO NATLEX, Online Burma/Myanmar Library, Myanmar Law Library, and UN ESCAP alongside official foreign reciprocity and consular bereavement guidance (travel.state.gov, GOV.UK, and the Embassy of Switzerland in Myanmar), with a practical warning that families must verify office hours and requirements directly with local Township Administration and Township Health authorities [1][2][3][5][6][8].

steps.title: Medical certification, post-mortems, and hospital storage constraints
steps.html:
• Hospital death notification and storage limits: Hospital doctors issue the initial medical record of death, while GOV.UK bereavement guidance notes that hospital mortuary cold storage is severely limited, suffers frequent power cuts, and facilities often request removal of the body within two days [2].
  • Mandatory post-mortems for foreign nationals: Under local practice in Myanmar, post-mortem examinations (autopsies) are generally required for deaths of non-Myanmar citizens regardless of whether the death appears natural, and police in the township routinely open an investigative file that can take months to close [2].
  • Release of personal belongings: Outside formal police investigations, personal effects are ordinarily released to the next of kin or authorized representative via local hospital or funeral-director coordination [2].

steps.title: Township civil registration and official death certificates
steps.html:
• Township Public Health and General Administration filing: Under Myanmar's civil registration system (historically anchored in the Births, Deaths and Marriages Registration Act 1943 and updated through the revised Vital Registration Manual), deaths are reported via Ward or Village Tract Administrators and registered through the Township Public Health Office and Township General Administration Department [1][4][5].
  • Local certificate issuance and language: The Township Medical Officer or public health office typically issues the official Burmese-language death certificate within one to two days of filing, though cause-of-death wording may remain brief [1][2][3].
  • Conflict-related access gaps: Ongoing hostilities and displacement prevent functioning civil registration in contested townships; families should preserve original hospital discharge summaries, Ward Administrator confirmation letters, and family household lists (Ein Daung Su Sayin) for delayed verification [1][5].

steps.title: Local burial, cremation, and Yangon airport repatriation
steps.html:
• Cremation and local burial permissions: Municipal crematoria operate in major cities such as Yangon and Mandalay, whereas local burial requires explicit permission from local township authorities and cemetery committees [2].
  • Repatriation through Yangon International Airport: Repatriating remains (or cremated ashes) out of Myanmar must pass through Yangon International Airport even if death occurred in another state or region, and requires a local civil death certificate, an embalming certificate, a body-transfer permit, and a consular covering letter [2][3].
  • Processing timelines and hospital clearance: Local repatriation formalities typically take eight to ten working days, and hospitals normally require full settlement of inpatient medical bills before releasing the body [2].

steps.title: Plural succession law, Burma Laws Act 1898, and probate courts
steps.html:
• Religion-based personal law rule: Under Section 13 of the Burma Laws Act (1898), inheritance and succession are decided according to personal religious law: Myanmar Customary Law governs Myanmar Buddhists (where children generally share equally and spouses hold recognized marital property interests, limiting unilateral wills), Islamic law governs Muslims, and Hindu law governs Hindus [6].
  • Succession Act 1925 and court probate: For Christians, Parsis, and civil estates or contested administration falling under the Succession Act (India Act XXXIX of 1925), families apply to District and Township Civil Courts (Probate and Succession) for probate of a will or Letters of Administration to access bank accounts and immovable property [7].
  • Certified translation for foreign estates: Because domestic civil and court records are issued in Burmese, families settling overseas assets need certified English translations attested locally before foreign use [1][2].

steps.title: Social Security Law 2012 benefits and consular legalization (non-Apostille)
steps.html:
• Social Security Board (SSB) funeral and survivor claims: Families of insured workers covered by the 2012 Social Security Law (Pyidaungsu Hluttaw Law No. 15/2012) should contact local Social Security Board (SSB) Township Offices (Social Security Law 2012) to inquire about statutory funeral grants and survivor pensions or lump-sum death benefits, noting operational disruptions across conflict-affected regions [8].
  • Non-Apostille treaty status: According to the Hague Conference on Private International Law (HCCH) status table, Myanmar is not a Contracting Party to the 1961 Hague Apostille Convention; Apostille certificates have no legal standing in or from Myanmar [9].
  • Consular legalization requirement: Using a Myanmar death certificate, court probate grant, or Power of Attorney abroad requires consular legalization: notarization and certified translation inside Myanmar, authentication by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs Consular Department (Naypyidaw / Yangon), and legalization by the receiving country's embassy [1][2][3][9].

contacts.name: Township Public Health Office and Township General Administration Department
contacts.note: Local township health and administrative offices recording deaths via Ward or Village Tract Administrators and issuing Burmese death certificates.

contacts.name: Social Security Board (SSB) Township Offices (Social Security Law 2012)
contacts.note: Administers insured workers' funeral grants, survivor pensions, and disability benefits under Pyidaungsu Hluttaw Law No. 15/2012.

contacts.name: District and Township Civil Courts (Probate and Succession)
contacts.note: Courts issuing Letters of Administration, probate orders, and succession rulings under the Burma Laws Act 1898 and Succession Act 1925.

contacts.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs Consular Department (Naypyidaw / Yangon)
contacts.note: Authenticates notarized Burmese and English civil documents, medical certificates, and court orders prior to foreign embassy legalization.
